title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 1)
text:
This document is going to be an extension of the Introduction to Drift Diffusion Models Github page. Thus, topics that were discussed thoroughly there will be covered more quickly through this document.
# Load in the packages
library(EMC2)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
# load in all custom ddm functions
source(here("ddm", "load.R"))

title: Simulating Go/No-Go Data
text:
library(EMC2)
set.seed(123)
factors <- list( subjects = paste0(“s”, 1:20), S = c(“go”, “nogo”) )
dGNG <- design( factors = factors, model = DDMGNG,
formula = list( v ~ S, a ~ 1, t0 ~ 1, Z ~ 1, sv ~ 1 ),
Rlevels = c(“RESP”, “TO”),
functions = list( TIMEOUT = function(d) rep(1.5, nrow(d)),
Rnogo = function(d)
  factor(rep("nogo", nrow(d)),
         levels = c("nogo", "go")),

Rgo = function(d)
  factor(rep("go", nrow(d)),
         levels = c("nogo", "go"))
) )

Get the parameters from the model
p_vector <- sampled_pars(dGNG)


Specify the parameters
p_vector[] <- c(1.5, -2.5, log(1.4), log(0.28), qnorm(0.5), log(0.4))


Simulate the data
sim_ddm_data <- make_data( parameters = p_vector, design = dGNG, n_trials = 400 )


FIX RESPONSE VARIABLE
sim_ddm_data\(R <- factor(
  ifelse(is.na(sim_ddm_data\)rt), “TO”, “RESP”), levels = c(“RESP”, “TO”) )


Print out the stimulus and response combination
(tab <- xtabs(~ S + R, sim_ddm_data)) addmargins(prop.table(tab, 1),2)
sim_ddm_data %>% group_by(S) %>% summarise(mean = mean(rt, na.rm = T), min = min(rt, na.rm = T), max = max(rt, na.rm = T))

title: Fitting a DDM to Go/No-Go Data
text:
2. Generating a Cumulative Defective Plot

2.1 Creating RT quantiles

# Specify the RT quantiles
rt_probs <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.2)

# Calculate RT quantiles separately for Go and No-Go responses
rt_quantiles <- gng %>%
  filter(R == "RESP") %>%
  group_by(S) %>%
  reframe(
    rt = quantile(rt, probs = rt_probs, na.rm = TRUE),
    quantile = rt_probs
  )

# Show the reaction time quantiles for go and ng trials
rt_quantiles

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   S        rt quantile
   <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>
 1 go     268       0.1
 2 go     293       0.3
 3 go     307       0.5
 4 go     324       0.7
 5 go     370.      0.9
 6 ng     268.      0.1
 7 ng     290.      0.3
 8 ng     301       0.5
 9 ng     314.      0.7
10 ng     335       0.9




2.2 Baking Accuracy into the RT Quantiles

# Calculate the probability of responding to each stimulus
response_probs <- gng %>%
  group_by(S) %>%
  reframe(
    p_response = mean(R == "RESP")
  )

# Convert the conditional RT quantiles to defective quantiles
defective_quantiles <- rt_quantiles %>%
  left_join(response_probs, by = "S") %>%
  mutate(
    defective_quantile = quantile * p_response
  )

# Show how accuracy influences the quantiles
defective_quantiles

# A tibble: 10 × 5
   S        rt quantile p_response defective_quantile
   <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>              <dbl>

10 ng     335       0.9       0.37              0.333




2.3 Plotting the RT Cumulative Defective Distribution

# Plot the defective RT distributions
defective_quantiles %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rt, y = defective_quantile, color = S, group = S)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative Defective Distribution for Subject 001 gng data",
    x = "Response Time (ms)",
    y = "Cumulative Response Probability",
    color = "Stimulus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

3. Fitting a Drift Diffusion Model (DDM)

3.1 Preparing the data for model fitting

# Introduce a subjects variable
gng <- mutate(gng, subjects = "001") %>% 
  relocate(subjects, .before = trial_num)

# convert variables to factors
gng <- mutate(gng,
              S = factor(S),
              R = factor(R))

# Convert reaction time into seconds
gng <- mutate(gng,
              rt = rt/1000)

# Specify the reference levels in the dataset
gng <- gng %>%
  mutate(
    R = factor(R, levels = c("TO", "RESP")),
    S = factor(S, levels = c("ng", "go"))
  )



3.2 Specifying a Design and Model

# Specifying the design and model object
dGNG <- design(

title: Introduction to Drift Diffusion Models
text:
To view a vignet from the EMC2 developers, please visit Drift Diffusion Model (DDM).
Note: The code below is a mixture from the code available in the MBNCS26 GitHub and some of my own custom functions available here:
# Load in the packages
library(EMC2)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
# load in all custom ddm functions
source(here("ddm", "load.R"))

title: Introduction to Drift Diffusion Models
text:
1. Simulating Two-Choice Data

1.1 Introduction to the design() function
We start by specifying what data we want to simulate using the design() function. Essentially, here we specify what the names of our factors are going to be, what covariates we may have, the levels of the responses, the model formula (indicating what DDM parameters we want to estimate), and the model itself.
We will start by generating this information for a Wiener diffusion model.
In this model, we are specifying the:

boundary separation (a)
the drift rate by stimulus (v)
the non-decision time (t0) and
the relative starting point (Z).

We are not estimating the intra-trial variability (s), the drift rate variability (sv), the relative starting point variability (SZ), nor the non-decision time variability (st0).
This is important because when we print ‘designWDM’, it doesn’t necessarily tell you what parameters are being estimated vs which ones are being fixed. However, we can tell that using the sampled_pars() function in the upcoming sections.
Also, for this type of model, the intra-trial (or within-trial) variability (s) is fixed to the value 1 rather than 0.1 like in Ratcliff’s version.

# Generating the data and model specification
designWDM <- design(model = DDM,
                    factors=list(subjects=1,S=1:2), # S is the stimulus 1, or 2
                    Rlevels = 1:2,                  # Corresponding responses
                    # Single value of each WDM parameter except rates
                    # where there is one value for each stimulus
                    formula = list(a ~ 1, 
                                   v ~ S, 
                                   t0 ~ 1, 
                                   Z ~ 1))

Parameter(s) s, st0, sv, SZ not specified in formula and assumed constant.



 Sampled Parameters: 
[1] "a"    "v"    "v_S2" "t0"   "Z"   

 Design Matrices: 
$a
 a
 1

$v
 S v v_S2
 1 1    0
 2 1    1

$t0
 t0
  1

$Z
 Z
 1

$s
 s
 1

$st0
 st0
   1

$sv
 sv
  1

$SZ
 SZ
  1




1.2 Using the mapped_pars() function
Below we can see the different condition-specific drift rates represented by the model using the mapped_pars() function. However, the model rewrites these drift rates in terms of the components that it will actually estimate. For example, for S1, it directly estimates the drift rate for this condition (v). For S2, rather than directly estimating its drift rate, it estimates the difference between the S2 and S1 drift rates (v_S2). The full drift rate for S2 is then represented as v + v_S2.
The model does this because we specified for it above when within formula we wrote v ~ S. By default it uses dummy coding and the v for S1 was chosen as the reference.

# Print out what parameters we want to estimate by factors
mapped_pars(designWDM)

$v 
  S  
 1  : v
 2  : v + v_S2




1.3 Specifyin DDM parameters using sampled_pars()
Here we are using sampled_pars() to extract an empty vector with the names of the parameters that will be estimated in the ddm. Within this empty vector, we add values that will inform the model on how to simulate the data, such as the drift rate, boundary separation, etc. Interestingly, several of these parameters will need to be transformed into a different scale to simulate the data as correctly. This includes boundary separation (a in log scale), non-decision time (t0 in log scale), and the relative starting point (Z in probit scale). This is done to make the data simulate and model estimation process more efficient. The drift rates, however, remain in the same scale.
Thus when we print out the chosen parameters, we see that the boundary separation (a) is the value 0, but this value is in the logit scale, so in the normal scale it is actually 1, and that is what we will see later on after we fit a ddm to the simulated data.
Another thing to note, notice that the drift rates we chose are -1 (v) and 2 (v_S2). We chose these values because we want the v drift rate to be -1 and the v_S2 drift rate to be 1. As shown in the previous section, the drift rates are being estimated by the stimulus factor using dummy coding, thus if we wrote in -1 and 1, as we inteded it, the drift rate of S2 would be specified as 0 (-1 + 1 = 0). To show this, we can use mapped_pars() again in combination with the design() object to show what we plan to simulate in the normal scale!

# Choose parameters for simulation, first getting a vector with the right name
parsWDM <- sampled_pars(designWDM)

# Then choosing some values. Note that we include transforms here to illustrate
# the scale on which sampling occurs
parsWDM[] <- c(log(1), -1, 2, log(.3), qnorm(.5))

# Here are the values
parsWDM

        a         v      v_S2        t0         Z 
 0.000000 -1.000000  2.000000 -1.203973  0.000000 

# Confirm our parameters were specified correctly
mapped_pars(designWDM, parsWDM)

  S  v a sv  t0 st0 s   Z SZ   z sz
1 1 -1 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0
2 2  1 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0




1.4 Simulate the data using make_data()
Now that we confirmed that we specified our parmeters correctly, we can use the make_data() function to simulate our two-choice dataset.

# Simulate the data
dat <- make_data(parameters = parsWDM, 
                 design = designWDM,
                 n_trials = 700) # Per stimulus

2. Visualizing the Data

2.1 Create a data_design() object
Inspired by the make_design() function from the EMC2 package, here we will be using the custom data_design() function to create an object that maps out the stimulus, response, and reaction time variables in the dataset, along with the rules that represent a correct response within stimulus.

# Create the data_design
dat_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == 1 & R == 1) | (S == 2 & R == 2),

)

title: Introduction to Drift Diffusion Models
text:
3. Specifying the Priors

3.1 Specifying the prior means
To specify the priors, we can use information from several studies that have identified what value ranges to expect for specific parameters. For example, we can use the work from Matzke and Wagenmakers (2009), to generate a table of these parameter value ranges for intra-trial noise being fixed to s = 0.1 or s = 1.0.









DDM Parameter
Psychological Meaning
Ratcliff (s = 0.1), min/max/mean
Other (s = 1.0), min/max/mean




Drift Rate (v)
Speed of information processing / task difficulty
0.000/0.586/0.223
0.00/5.86/2.23


Boundary Separation (a)
Response caution / distance to decision threshold
0.056/0.393/0.125
0.56/3.93/1.25


Absolute Starting Point (z)
A priori bias toward one response
0.028/0.182/0.063
0.28/1.82/0.63


Relative Starting Point (z/a)
Relative starting point (0.5 = unbiased)
0.272/0.782/0.500
0.272/0.782/0.500


Nondecision Time (Ter)
Sensory encoding + motor execution time (in seconds)
0.206/0.942/0.435s
0.206/0.942/0.435s


Drift Rate Variability (Sv)
Across-trial variability in drift rate
0.000/0.329/0.133
0.00/3.29/1.33


Starting Point Variability (Sz)
Across-trial variability in starting point
0.000/0.169/0.037
0.00/1.69/0.37


Nondecision Time Variability (St)
Across-trial variability in nondecision time (in seconds)
0.000/0.630/0.183s
0.000/0.630/0.183s



Notice how the intra-trial noise essentially works as a scaling variable, and that this has an effect on all non-time related parameters. It does not affect the time parameters since it already has seconds as units of measurement.
From the information in the table above, we can use the reported means to inform the means for our priors!

# Specify the prior means in the transformed scale
pmean <- c(
  a = log(1.25), 
  v = -2.2, 
  v_S2 = 2.2,  
  t0 = log(.4),
  Z = qnorm(.5) 
)



3.2 Specifying the prior standard deviations
Additionally, we can use the table to inform the spread for our parameters. Now, the spread will be in the transformed scale. We can essentially use the following formula to calculate the standard deviation for most of the parameters:
\[SD = \frac{\text{MAX} - \text{MIN}}{4}\] For example, starting with the boundary separation (a), we know that across studies it ranges between 0.56 and 3.93 in the untransformed scale. Therefore, we need to pick a value in the log scale that keeps the values restricted within this range. To do this, we can just log transform these values to produce log(0.56) = -0.58 and log(3.93) = 1.36. We can take the difference to get the range = 1.36 - (-0.58) = 1.94. We can then divide this number by 4 to get a rough estimate of the standard deviation = 1.94/4 = 0.49.
Similarly, for non-decision time, we can use the same formula ((log(0.942) - log(0.206))/4 = 0.38), and the same for the relative starting point ((qnorm(0.782) - qnorm(0.272))/4 = 0.35).
Lastly, while following the same formula for the drift parameters results in 5.86/4 = 1.47, this value might be a bit too restrictive. It will likely work well in most cases where the data look good, however, in situations where the performers are quite poor, using a much larger value like 2.5 would work much better.

# Standard deviations
psd <- c(
  a = 0.5,     # Spread for log(a)
  v = 2.5,     # Spread for drift rate v (S1)
  v_S2 = 2.5,  # Spread for drift rate v (S2)
  t0 = 0.38,   # Spread for log(t0)
  Z = 0.35     # Spread for probit(Z)
)



3.3 Combining the prior means and standard deviations
Now we can combine the prior means with the prior standard deviations, along with the model design that indicates how we will specify the model (review section 1.1) to create our priors which are saved within an ‘emc.prior’ object.
Below we can view these means and the variances (standard deviations^2). Additionally we can pair this with the summary() function to confirm that the covariances among the parameters were specified to zero.

# We can use the "prior" function to combine this information, indicting that
# the prior is at the single subject level.
priorWDM <- prior(designWDM,
                  pmean=pmean, 
                  psd=psd,
                  type="single") # Non-hierarchical

class(priorWDM)

[1] "emc.prior"

priorWDM

Mean and variance of the prior on the transformed parameters: 
a ~ 𝑁(0.22, 0.25)
v ~ 𝑁(-2.2, 6.25)
v_S2 ~ 𝑁(2.2, 6.25)
t0 ~ 𝑁(-0.92, 0.14)
Z ~ 𝑁(0, 0.12)

For detailed info use summary(<prior>)

# To see the 0 covariances as well:
summary(priorWDM)

alpha  -  Subject-level prior 

mean of the prior :

 0.2231436 -2.2000000  2.2000000 -0.9162907  0.0000000 
variance of the prior :

a    0.25 0.00 0.00 0.0000 0.0000

3.4 Plotting the prior distributions
Below we can plot the prior distributions in the transformed scale, this is essentially showing the numbers that we deliberately specified in the previos section. We also have the option to extract the values, in case we wanted to generate these plots using ggplot() or wanted to do something else with the values. More importantly, we can also plot the prior distribution in the natural scale, which is much more informative to see if we specified everything correctly.

plot(priorWDM, designWDM, map=FALSE, layout=c(2,4))

title: Introduction to Drift Diffusion Models
text:
4. Fitting the Drift Diffusion Model

4.1 Making an emc object
Before we can fit the DDM, we need to create an emc object, where we specify what data we are trying to fit the model to, what the design is (basically what parameters we want to estimate and how vs fixed), if the model is hierarchical or not (single means no while standard means yes), and what the prior distributions are.
When we print out the object, it basically shows us 0’s for the preburn, burn, adapt, and sample stage. This table essentially tracks the EMC2’s Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation for the four sampling stages.

preburn: A broad initial search of the parameter space
burn: MCMC chains run until preliminary convergence criteria are met
adapt: Samples are gathered to construct proposal distributions for efficient sampling
sample: The final posterior samples

For more information on what these four sampling stages mean, please visit: Day1-BasicEAMs/2-Dual.R
Additionally, we get a message of a likelihood speedup factor, which represents EMC2’s RT quantization. Essentially, instead of calculating likelihoods for all trials in the data, it instead creates response time bins of unique trial types and runs the likelihood for those. This speeds up the calculation time while not sacrificing accuracy.

# Create an emc object
sWDM <-  make_emc(data = dat, 
                  design = designWDM, 
                  type="single",
                  prior=priorWDM)

Processing data set 1


Likelihood speedup factor: 8 (176 unique trials)

# Print the object
sWDM

Iterations: 
     preburn burn adapt sample
[1,]       0    0     0      0
[2,]       0    0     0      0
[3,]       0    0     0      0

Subjects: 
[1] "1"

Parameters: 
[1] "a"    "v"    "v_S2" "t0"   "Z"   




4.2 Fitting the DDM model
In our example the model took only a few seconds to run, however this will not always be the case so it is recommended to save your model object and then load it in to save time in the future.
The code here is very straightforward, we use use the fit() function and we will see outputs indicating how each of the four sampling stages went.
By default, the fit() function will use three independent chains for the sampling process. The model is fit using parallel processing, where one core is devoted to one of the chains. You cannot increase the parallel processing speed by adding more cores than chains being used.

# Fitting the model
#sWDM <- fit(sWDM)

# Saving the model object
#save(sWDM, file = here("ddm", "models", "sWDM.Rdata"))

# Loading the model object
load(here("ddm", "models", "sWDM.Rdata"))

# Check the class
class(sWDM)

[1] "emc"




4.3 Checking model convergence using check()
It doesn’t really make sense to interpret the parameter estimates unless we can verify that the model converged correctly. We can confirm that the model converged by using the check() function, where we are informed how many chains and samples are within each chain under iterations, along with the R hat and ESS values.
The R hat values measure chain convergence, by comparing the variance within individual MCMC chains to the variance between different chains. Basically if this value is less than 1.1, then that means there are very little differences between the chains, which is good since they are all in the same sampling space essentially.
The effective sample size (ESS) tells us the number of independent samples drawn from the posterior distribution after accounting for autocorrelation between successive MCMC iterations. Thus, higher ESS means lower autocorrelation, which is a good thing. I think having more than 400 (regardless of number of chains or samples within chains) is considered the bare minimum and having around 1000 means you are pretty good to go.
In our specific example, since we had 3 MCMC chains where each have 1000 samples, for a total of 3000 samples, the fact that parameters v and Z have 3000 for ESS show essentially all samples achieved full independence with no autocorrelation.
Lastly, the check() function also produces these fuzzy caterpillar plots, where if the plot looks like a fuzzy caterpillar (as shown below) that convergence was successful. It produces this plot for the parameter with the highest R hat in the model.

check(sWDM)

Iterations:
     preburn burn adapt sample
[1,]       0    0     0   1000
[2,]       0    0     0   1000
[3,]       0    0     0   1000

 1 
        a        v v_S2       t0    Z
Rhat    1    1.001    1    1.001    1
ESS  2887 3000.000 2811 2494.000 3000











4.4 Extracting Model Parameter Estimates
Since everything looked okay, we can now go ahead and extract the model parameter estimates. There are a couple ways of doing this, the first is to use the summary() function which produces the estimates in the transformed scale along with their corresponding R hat and ESS values. For example, the boundary separation (a) is in the log scale while the relative starting point (Z) is in the probit scale. A better approach would instead be to use the credint() function with the ‘map=TRUE’ argument to return them the estimates in the natural scale, making them much easier to interpret.
Essentially, how Bayesian statistics work is that it generates multiple combinations of estimated parameters (e.g., a = 1.01, v_S1 = -1.2, v_S2 = 1.01, t0 = .288, Z = .512) and examines how well that explains the data by examining the produced likelihood value from that combination It then does this over and over again and when the likelihood value remains similar across different parameter combination values, then the model has converged. However, since we have many combinations, we can essentially create distributions within each parameter of these values, which are known as the posterior distributions. Since we have 3 chains, each with 1,000 samples, then every parameter in our model will have a distribution of 3,000 values. From this distribution, the median is going to represent the reported parameter estimate, basically the value at 50% of the distribution, while the values at 2.5% and 97.5% represent our certainty or our 95% credible interval. We can essentially extract for each parameter those values down below with both the summary() and credint() functions.

# Getting model parameter estimates using summary()
summary(sWDM)

t0   -1.254 -1.242 -1.232 1.001 2494
Z    -0.040  0.004  0.051 1.000 3000

# Getting model parameter estimates using credint()
credint(sWDM, selection="alpha", map=TRUE)

section: 5. Does the model capture the data well?
text:
5. Does the model capture the data well?

5.1 Producing the predicted (fitted) values
We can now use the predict() function on the emc object that contains the model information. This code can also take a while to run sometimes, but not as long as fitting the actual model. Regardless, it is also recommended to save the predicted values and load them to save on time.
Interestingly, unlike the fitted() function which produces a vector of fitted values for a regression, the predict() function in our case produces a data frame, where the trial information essentially represents predicted information. For example, down below the variables subjects and S should match the same dimensions as our original data- think of them as fixed predictors. However, the R and rt variables are different, because those two variables are the fitted values.
To illustrate this, the second table shows how the trials, S, and subjects variable from the predicted dataset matches that of the original but the R and rt variables differ. This makes sense since having different R and rt values represents how the model parameters are explaining data accuracy and reaction time.
Lastly, by default the predict() function produces fitted trials, the same number as the original dataset for the same number of stimulus types (in our case 700 for S1 and 700 for S2), but it does so 50 times. This is formally called posterior predictives or posterior predictive datasets. This just means that the fitted trials are generated by drawing parameter values from a posterior distribution.
In other words, the predict() function is picking parameter estimates at random from their posterior distribution and using that information to generate the fitted trials. Afterwards, it picks another random set of parameter value combinations from their posterior distributions, produces fitted values and repeats the process (at default it does this 50 times). Also, notice that each reaction time value is slightly different from each other even under the same conditions (same S and R), this is due to the added randomness to that trail from the fixed ‘s’ parameter, which represents the within-trial (intra-trial) variability. Conceptually, you can think of this as the squiggly line that can push a decision earlier or later than the drift rate (average time it takes to make a decision for a specific stimulus).
Each iteration is differentiated by the ‘postn’ variable. From this predicted information, we can calculate means for predicted accuracy and reaction time to see if it is capturing the data well, while also allowing us to investigate how close the predicted values across iterations are to each other. More specifically, we can use the 50 replicates to construct 95% credible intervals.

# Use the predict function to obtain the fitted values
#ppWDM <- predict(sWDM)

# Saving the predicted object
#saveRDS(ppWDM, file = here("ddm", "predicted_values", "ppWDM.rds"))

ppWDM <- readRDS(here("ddm", "predicted_values", "ppWDM.rds"))

5.2 Plotting the Predicted Values
Now this is where things get interesting. In continuation of our previous section where we produced fitted trials for 50 iterations, we can now use this information to generate plots for our original dataset and our predicted datasets to see how well the model captures the raw data. We can do this in two ways, by creating defective density plots or defective cumulative distribution function plots- both tell us essentially the same information.
For the former, we can use the plot_density() function, where we specify the original dataset, the predicted datasets, and the factors we are interested in faceting the graphs (in our case just stimulus). Essentially, the plot produces defective density plots for both stimuli, just like we produced in section 2.3, for the original or raw data as black lines. These plots represent the distribution of reaction time where all possible responses (for a DDM there are two, in our case R1 and R2) where separately they do not integrate to one but together they do within a specific stimulus. In other words, it has accuracy baked into the distribution!
It then plots the 50% median values from the predicted datasets as defective density plots (green lines), allowing us to compare how similar to the distribution of both black and green lines are to each other. Moreover, since we have 50 predicted datasets, we can create distributions of reaction times for a stimulus and response combination at a specific quantile for reaction time (e.g., S1 and R1 at 1.1 RT), obtain the values at 2.5 and 97.5% for the specific RT location, and use that to essentially generate a 95% credible interval. We then do this across all stimulus and response combinations (in our case there are 4) for each value of RT to produce a full 95% credible interval.
The logic then is the following, if our Bayesian DDM model is doing a good job at explaining our data, then our data defective distributions should be within the 95% credible interval of the predicted datasets. Looking at the plot below, it looks like it does!
Similarly, we can also plot this information as defective cumulative distribution functions using the plot_cdf() function, again we see that the original data falls within the 95% credible interval created by the predicted datasets.

# plotting predicted values as a density plot
plot_density(dat, ppWDM, factors = c("S"))







# Plotting the predicted values as a cumulative defective function
plot_cdf(dat, ppWDM, factors = c("S"))










5.3 Quickly Checking Accuracy
The code below is more of a proof of concept, showing essentially that we can use the aggregate() function to quickly get a sense of accuracy in the data. However, what is important below is the order in which we aggregate information, especially for the predicted datasets. Notice that the last thing we average out is postn, this was done by design as removing it early in the calculate will produce incorrect means.

# Getting descriptives for the original data
agg1 <- aggregate(R=="2"~subjects*S, dat, mean)
colnames(agg1)[3] <- c("pR2")
agg2 <- aggregate(pR2~S, agg1, mean)

# Getting descriptives for the predicted datasets
agg1_pp <- aggregate(R=="2"~ S*subjects*postn, ppWDM, mean)
colnames(agg1_pp)[4] <- c("pR2")
agg2_pp <- aggregate(pR2~S*postn, agg1_pp, mean)
agg3_pp <- aggregate(pR2~S, agg2_pp, median)
low_pp <- aggregate(pR2~S, agg2_pp, function(x) quantile(x, 0.025))
upp_pp <- aggregate(pR2~S, agg2_pp, function(x) quantile(x, 0.975))

agg4_pp <- data.frame(
  S      = agg3_pp$S,
  "2.5%"  = low_pp$pR2,
  "50%"   = agg3_pp$pR2,
  "97.5%" = upp_pp$pR2,
  check.names = FALSE  
)

title: Introduction to Drift Diffusion Models
text:
6. Parameter Recovery

6.1 Simulating data from our model parameters
In the previous section, the goal was to use the predict() function to simulate trials and then compare how the simulated data compares to the original data. For this section, we are doing something different. This time, we are treating the median (50%) parameter estimates as the ground truth and are a) simulating data using these parameters and then b) fitting the same DDM model to this simulated dataset to see if we can get similar parameter estimates to what we initially got from the initial posterior distribution. This process is known as parameter recovery and must be done to confirm that our model is reliable to interpret.
Why do this? Well because with evidence accumulation models (EAMs), it is possible to recreate the data well using completely different values for the EAMs parameters. In such case, that invalidates the original interpretation of the data- thus this needs to be done in order to see if your estimates remain consistent or not. In other words, what we did before with the predict() function can produce datasets that look just like the original, but both originate from different estimated values, which is bad for us when it comes to interpreting the model.
Anyway to do this, we first start by using the made_data() function, which we have already have done in section 1.4. Again, this takes in the inputs of the parameters, in our case we can just insert the emc object with our model output, the design object that has the model specification, and our original dataset, so that the simulated data keeps the same structure (e.g., number of trials).

# Simulate data from our model parameters
sim <- make_data(parameters = sWDM,
                 design = designWDM,
                 data=dat)



6.2 Fitting the DDM to the simulated data
In this section, we fit the DDM model to our simulated dataset. Just like before, we start by creating an emc object using the make_emc() function and then fitting the model using fit().
Since fitting a DDM can take a long time, it is also adviced here to save the model output and then load that in.

# Make an emc object
sim_sWDM <- make_emc(data = sim,
                     design = designWDM,
                     type="single",
                     prior = priorWDM)

Processing data set 1


Likelihood speedup factor: 7.6 (184 unique trials)

# Fit the model to the simulated data
# sim_sWDM <- fit(sim_sWDM)

# Saving the model object
# save(sim_sWDM, file = here("ddm", "models", "sim_sWDM.Rdata"))

# Loading the model object
load(here("ddm", "models", "sim_sWDM.Rdata"))



6.3 Checking the parameter recovery
Lastly, we use the credint() function to extract the estimated parameters (50th percentile of the posterior distribution) in the transformed scale and save it as a vector.
Next, we use the recovery() function to perform the parameter recovery study. It creates a diagnostic scatterplot for each DDM parameter that was estimated and also provides a correlation coefficient and an RMSE value. If the correlation is larger than .75 then that is considered good recovery and if its larger than 90 then that is considered excellent recovery (Myers et al. 2022; White et al., 2018b).
In our example, we got r = 0.998, which is phenomenal. The RMSE is not that important.

# Save the original parameters from the model (in transformed scale)
ground_truth_params <- credint(sWDM)[[1]][,"50%"]

# Compare parameters from the original to the simulated data
recovery(emc = sim_sWDM, 
         true_pars = ground_truth_params)

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models
section: 1. Can a DDM Capure Go/No-Go data?
text:
1. Can a DDM Capure Go/No-Go data?
The following section is inspired by the work of Ratcliff et al., 2016. Essentilly, we are going to replicate their work by simulating two choice data, turning it into Go/No-Go (GnG) data by removing reaction times from a response, and then fitting a DDM to the two choice and a GnG DDM to the GnG and seeing if the parameters are similar to each other or not.
Why do this? Well since it is the exact same dataset that is just being manipulated to not have a response time, then mathematically, the DDM should be able to generate the same parameter estimates that was used to generate it.

1.1 Specifying the DDM and GnG DDM
We first start by using the design() function to specify the models we want to use. We will specify both a regular and GnG DDM model, using only the regular to simulate the data. Again for a review on the regular DDM model, please visit introduction to DDM linked at the top of the page.
For the GnG DDM model, there is more information that we need to specify. For starters, we need to use the ‘DDMGNG’ model within the design() function, which expects missing reaction times as a legitimate response (or in this case lack of a response). The factors argument tells the function information about our data that does not exist yet, but that is needed to know for this function to work (e.g., subjects and stimulus). For the Rlevels argument, we need to specify what the two response values are, we chose “RESP” and “TO” but this is arbitrary. Next we specify what paramerers we want to estimated from the GnG DDM, we chose the same ones as for the two-choice DDM. Then we now have to specify information within the functions argument. The TIMEOUT represents essentially the reaction time threshold in seconds, when a non-response was given. Next, the Rnogo argument is where we tell the design() function what the level name for R is that represents a no-go response. Similarly, the Rgo argument is the level name for R that represents a response.

# Generating the data and model specification
designWDM <- design(model = DDM,
                    factors=list(subjects=1, S=1:2), 
                    Rlevels = 1:2,                  
                    formula = list(a ~ 1, 
                                   v ~ S, 
                                   t0 ~ 1, 
                                   Z ~ 1)) 

# Generating the model specifications for a GnG dataset
designWDM_gng <- design(model = DDMGNG,
                        factors=list(subjects=1, S=c("go", "ng")),
                        Rlevels = c("RESP", "TO"),
                        formula = list(a ~ 1,
                                       v ~ S, 
                                       t0 ~ 1,
                                       Z ~ 1),
                        functions = list(
                          TIMEOUT = function(d) rep(1.5, nrow(d)),
                          Rnogo  = function(d) factor(rep("TO",   nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP")),
                          Rgo    = function(d) factor(rep("RESP", nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP"))
                        ))



1.2 Simulating the Two-Choice and GnG Data

# Choose parameters for simulation, first getting a vector with the right name
parsWDM <- sampled_pars(designWDM)

# Then choosing some values. Note that we include transforms here to illustrate
# the scale on which sampling occurs
parsWDM[] <- c(log(1), -1, 2.8, log(.3), qnorm(.5))

# Confirm our parameters were specified correctly
mapped_pars(designWDM, parsWDM)

  S    v a sv  t0 st0 s   Z SZ   z sz
1 1 -1.0 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0
2 2  1.8 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0

# Simulate the two-choide data
dat <- make_data(parameters = parsWDM, 
                 design = designWDM,
                 n_trials = 1000) # Per stimulus 

# Convert the data into GnG data
gng <- dat %>%
  mutate(S = ifelse(S == "1", "go", "ng"),
         R = ifelse(R == "2", "TO", "RESP"),
         rt = ifelse(R == "TO", NA, rt))



1.3 Visualizing both datasets

# Create the data_design for the two choice and one for the gng
dat_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == 1 & R == 1) | (S == 2 & R == 2),
  id = subjects
)

gng_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == "go" & R == "RESP") | (S == "ng" & R == "TO"),

)

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models
text:
1. Simulating Two-Choice and GNG Data
The following section is inspired by the work of Ratcliff et al. (2018). Essentially, we are going to replicate their work by simulating two choice data (2C), turning it into Go/No-Go data (GNG) by removing reaction times from a response, and then fitting a DDM to the 2C and a GNG DDM to the GNG and seeing if the parameters are similar to each other or not.
Why do this? Well since it is the exact same dataset that is just being manipulated to not have a response time, then mathematically, the DDM should be able to generate the same parameter estimates that was used to generate it.

1.1 Specifying the DDM and GNG DDM
We first start by using the design() function to specify the models we want to use. For both models, we will use the Wiener diffusion model (WDM), so that abbreviation will be used for the models. This just means that these DDMs will not estimate between-trial variability parameters (e.g., Sv, St0, SZ).
For the GNG DDM model, there is more information that we need to specify. For starters, we need to specify the ‘DDMGNG’ model within the design() function, which expects missing reaction times as a legitimate response (or in this case lack of a response). The factors argument tells the function information about our data that does not exist yet, but that is needed to know for this function to work (e.g., subjects and stimulus). For the Rlevels argument, we need to specify what the two response values are, we chose “TO” and “RESP” but this is arbitrary.
It is important to note that reference level of the factors will be used as the lower boundary in this model. Therefore, it is important to have “TO” as the reference (first level) for Rlevels and also to code “ng” as the reference for S.
Next we specify what parameters we want to estimate from the GNG DDM, which is the ones we estimate from a WDM. Additionally, we now have to code for information within the functions argument. The TIMEOUT represents essentially the reaction time threshold in seconds when a non-response was given- this doesn’t really matter (I don’t think) since we are changing the reaction times to NAs anyway. Next, the Rnogo argument is where we tell the design() function what the level name for R is that represents a no-go response. Similarly, the Rgo argument is the level name for R that represents a response.

# Generating the data and model specification
designWDM <- design(model = DDM,
                    factors=list(subjects=1, S=1:2), 
                    Rlevels = 1:2,                  
                    formula = list(a ~ 1, 
                                   v ~ S, 
                                   t0 ~ 1, 
                                   Z ~ 1)) 

# Generating the model specifications for a GnG dataset
designWDMGNG <- design(model = DDMGNG,
                       factors=list(subjects=1, S=c("ng", "go")),
                       Rlevels = c("TO", "RESP"),
                       formula = list(a ~ 1,
                                       v ~ S, 
                                       t0 ~ 1,
                                       Z ~ 1),
                      functions = list(
                          TIMEOUT = function(d) rep(1.5, nrow(d)),
                          Rnogo  = function(d) factor(rep("TO",   nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP")),
                          Rgo    = function(d) factor(rep("RESP", nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP"))
                        ))



1.2 Simulating the Two-Choice and GNG Data
Important: We chose a large number of trials (n = 5000 for each S) to simulate in order to get really good parameter recovery. Here we are using the sampled_pars() function to extract a vector with the parameter names which then we populate with the values chosen below in their respective transformed scale.
We use mapped_pars() to confirm we specified the parameter values correctly and then we simulate the data using the make_data() function.
Afterwards, we take the simulated two-choice data and just change it to resemble a GnG dataset. Keep in mind, there are GnG data simulating specific functions but we are not showing that in this document. This is, however, available in Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 2).

# Choose parameters for simulation, first getting a vector with the right name
parsWDM <- sampled_pars(designWDM)

# Then choosing some values. Note that we include transforms here to illustrate
# the scale on which sampling occurs
parsWDM[] <- c(log(1), -.75, 3.4, log(.3), qnorm(.5))

# Confirm our parameters were specified correctly
mapped_pars(designWDM, parsWDM)

  S     v a sv  t0 st0 s   Z SZ   z sz
1 1 -0.75 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0
2 2  2.65 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0

# Simulate the two-choide data
dat <- make_data(parameters = parsWDM, 
                 design = designWDM,
                 n_trials = 5000) # Per stimulus 

# Convert the two-choice data into GnG data
gng <- dat %>%
  mutate(S = ifelse(S == "1", "ng", "go"),
         R = ifelse(R == "1", "TO", "RESP"),
         rt = ifelse(R == "TO", NA, rt))

# Convert variables to factors (MUST DO THIS OR fit() will FAIL)
gng <- gng %>%
  mutate(
    S = factor(S, levels = c("ng", "go")),
    R = factor(R, levels = c("TO", "RESP"))
  )



1.3 Visualizing both datasets
We can use my custom functions to create a data_design object so that we can then use the functions get_descriptives() and the plotting functions plot_defectiveDensity() and plot_defectiveDensityGNG() on our datasets.
Since they are essentially the same data, we see that the accuracy and reaction times between the two are identical. Important to note, the function of the plot_defectiveDensity() function is to produce defective density plots for each stimuli in the dataset. This plot, however, makes no sense for the GnG, since within a stimulus, there is only one response with a reaction time! Thus, it is more informative to instead compare the RT distributions between stimuli, which is what the plot_defectiveDensityGNG() function does.

# Create the data_design for the two choice data
dat_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == 1 & R == 1) | (S == 2 & R == 2),
  id = subjects
)

# Create the data_design for the gng data
gng_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == "go" & R == "RESP") | (S == "ng" & R == "TO"),
  id = subjects

section: 2. Fitting a DDM and GnG DDM to the data
text:
2. Fitting a DDM and GnG DDM to the data

2.1 Generating prior distributions
A deeper review for these values in terms of means and standard deviations is available in the introduction to DDM guide. Note that for our purposes, we are using the same prior distribution for the two-choice and gng data. However, in practice we would expect these distributions to be different, since the GnG task itself generally results in different parameter values compared to the two-choice (e.g., higher drift rate for go trials while weaker drift rate for no-go trials).
However, we do need to construct two ‘emc.prior’ objects using the prior() function since they require a model design object. In other words, failing to do this will cause errors during the fitting process.

# Specify the prior means in the transformed scale
pmean <- c(
  a = log(1.25), 
  v = -2.2, 
  v_S2 = 2.2,  
  t0 = log(.4),
  Z = qnorm(.5) 
)

# Standard deviations
psd <- c(
  a = 0.5,     # Spread for log(a)
  v = 2.5,     # Spread for drift rate v (S1)
  v_S2 = 2.5,  # Spread for drift rate v (S2)
  t0 = 0.38,   # Spread for log(t0)
  Z = 0.35     # Spread for probit(Z)
)

# Generating the prior distributions for the two-choice data
priorWDM <- prior(design=designWDM,
                  pmean=pmean, 
                  psd=psd,
                  type="single") # Non-hierarchical

# Generating the prior distributions for the gng data
priorWDMGNG <- prior(design=designWDMGNG,
                     pmean=pmean, 
                     psd=psd,
                     type="single") # Non-hierarchical

# plotting on the natural scale
plot(priorWDM, designWDM, layout=c(2,4))










2.2 Fitting the two models
To fit the models we first need to create emc objects using the make_emc() function. The input for this function is the data, the model design, the priors, and whether the model is hierarchical or not. Notice the names from these different inputs have to be compatible with each other, this is why for the gng, we needed to have its own model design and its own specific prior distribution.
After that we use the fit() function to run the Bayesian model, which can take a while so it is recommended to save the output once the model is done and then load it back into R.
Here we are naming the models as WDM, to remind us they are Wiener’s DDM and we separate them by the task (2 choice = 2C; GnG = GNG)

# Create an emc object for the two-choice data
sWDM_2C <-  make_emc(data = dat, 
                     design = designWDM, 
                     type="single",
                     prior=priorWDM)

Processing data set 1


Likelihood speedup factor: 44.2 (226 unique trials)

# Create an emc object for the gng data
sWDM_GNG <-  make_emc(data = gng, 
                      design = designWDMGNG, 
                      type= "single",
                      prior=priorWDMGNG)

# Loading the model objects

Using the check() function we can see that both models converged nicely. The Rhat values are less than 1.1, which is good! Additionally all of the ESS values are much larger than 1,000. For a review on the interpretation of these values, please visit the introduction to DDM guide.

Here we use the mapped_pars() function to remind ourselves what parameter values were chose (ground truth) to simulate the data. With the credint() function, we can see that both the regular DDM and the GnG DDM recovered essentially the same parameters!

text:
4. Parameter Recovery
We now need to confirm that we can recover the parameters from the GNG WDM. This is because it is possible to generate data similar to our original data from multiple combinations of parameter estimates. Thus, if we can recover very similar parameters from simulated data using our initial model estimates, then that means we can be more confident our model is working as intended.
Anyway, here we use the make_data() function to simulate data using the GNG WDM estimated parameters, turn it into an emc object and then fit the model to it.

# Simulate data from our model parameters
sim <- make_data(parameters = sWDM_GNG,
                 design = designWDMGNG,
                 data=gng)

# Make an emc object
sim_sWDM_GNG <- make_emc(data = sim,
                         design = designWDMGNG,
                         type="single",
                         prior = priorWDMGNG)

Processing data set 1


Likelihood speedup factor: 88.5 (113 unique trials)

# Fit the model to the simulated data
# sim_sWDM_GNG <- fit(sim_sWDM_GNG)

# Saving the model object
# save(sim_sWDM_GNG, file = here("ddm", "models", "sim_sWDM_GNG.Rdata"))

# Loading the model object
load(here("ddm", "models", "sim_sWDM_GNG.Rdata"))

Here we use the recovery() function to assess how similar the parameters from the original GNG WDM and the one fit to the simulated data are to each other. It is a perfect recovery.

# Save the original parameters from the model (in transformed scale)
ground_truth_params <- credint(sWDM_GNG)[[1]][,"50%"]

# Compare parameters from the original to the simulated data
recovery(emc = sim_sWDM_GNG, 
         true_pars = ground_truth_params)

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 2)
text:
This document is going to be an extension of the Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 1) Github page. There are two main sections to this document. The first part discusses how to simulate Go/No-Go (GNG) data directly rather than transforming simulated two-choice data into a GNG, how to specify GNG prior distributions from the existing literature, and how to fit a GNG DDM along with model checking. In the second part, we fit GNG DDMs to a GNG task that was completed twice by me (Leo), where in one condition, I tried to do the task as quickly as possible and in another, as accurate as possible. These data along with their estimated DDM parameters are explored in this section.
# load in packages
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(EMC2)
# load in all custom ddm functions
source(here("ddm", "load.R"))

text:
1. Simulating GnG Data

# Generating the model specifications for a GnG dataset
designWDM_gng <- design(model = DDMGNG,
                        factors=list(subjects=1, S=c("ng", "go")),
                        Rlevels = c("TO", "RESP"),
                        formula = list(a ~ 1,
                                       v ~ S, 
                                       t0 ~ 1,
                                       Z ~ 1),
                        functions = list(
                          TIMEOUT = function(d) rep(1.5, nrow(d)),
                          Rnogo  = function(d) factor(rep("TO",   nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP")),
                          Rgo    = function(d) factor(rep("RESP", nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP"))
                        ))


# Choose parameters for simulation, first getting a vector with the right name
parsWDM_gng <- sampled_pars(designWDM_gng)

# Then choosing some values. Note that we include transforms here to illustrate
# the scale on which sampling occurs
parsWDM_gng[] <- c(log(1), -1, 4.2, log(.3), qnorm(.5))

# Confirm our parameters were specified correctly
mapped_pars(designWDM_gng, parsWDM_gng)

   S TIMEOUT Rnogo  Rgo    v a sv  t0 st0 s   Z SZ   z sz TIMEOUT.1 Rnogo.1
1 ng     1.5    TO RESP -1.0 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0       1.5       1
2 go     1.5    TO RESP  3.2 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0       1.5       1


We are using Ratcliff et al., 2018 same data structure for their study, where their GnG task had 960 trials for each subject, where 720 trials were ‘go’ trials (75%) and 240 trials (25%) were ‘no-go’ trials.

# Specify task structure
n_trials <- 960
prop_nogo <- 0.25

# Calculate number of Go and No-Go trials
n_nogo <- round(n_trials * prop_nogo)
n_go   <- n_trials - n_nogo

# Create simulation framework
gng_framework <- data.frame(
  trials = seq_len(n_trials),
  subjects = factor(1),
  S = factor(
    sample(c(rep("go", n_go), rep("ng", n_nogo))),
    levels = c("ng", "go")
  ),
  R = factor(
    rep(NA_character_, n_trials),
    levels = c("TO", "RESP")
  )
)


# Simulate the gng data
gng <- make_data(data = gng_framework,
                 parameters = parsWDM_gng, 
                 design = designWDM_gng)

# Specify the prior means in the transformed scale
pmean <- c(
  a = log(1.31), 
  v = -1.8, 
  v_Sgo = 2.5,  
  t0 = log(.38),
  Z = qnorm(.57) 
)



2.2 Specifying prior standard deviations for a GNG
In the introduction to the DDM document, we used the following rule to calculate prior standard deviations (a heuristic):
\[ SD = \frac{\text{MAX} - \text{MIN}}{4}\] The problem is, when we did that we had estimates nicely summarized for us from a study that reviewed 23 DDM studies. In our case, we reported parameter estimates from literally 4 studies- thus using the formula above, while informative, might lead us to have very restricted ranges. Instead, what we can do is keep the same logic but change the denominator from 4 down to 2 for now, until there are more studies available or someone nicely summerizes it all for us.
\[ SD_{GNG} = \frac{\text{MAX} - \text{MIN}}{2}\]
boundary separation (a): (log(1.620) - log(0.990))/2 = 0.25 non-decision time (Ter): (log(0.474) - log(0.253))/2 = 0.31 relative-starting point (Z): (qnorm(0.691) - qnorm(0.402))/2 = 0.37
We purposly kept the drift rates wide (2.5) rather than using the formula above, just in case we have very poor performers in our datasets. The same decision was made when specifying the prior distribution for the 2C DDM.

# Standard deviations for the GNG priors
psd <- c(
  a = 0.25,     # Spread for log(a)
  v = 2.5,     # Spread for drift rate v (ng)
  v_Sgo = 2.5,  # Spread for drift rate v (go)
  t0 = 0.31,   # Spread for log(t0)
  Z = 0.37     # Spread for probit(Z)
)

# Standard deviations from the 2C DDM priors
#psd <- c(
#  a = 0.5,     # Spread for log(a)
#  v = 2.5,     # Spread for drift rate v (S1)
#  v_S2 = 2.5,  # Spread for drift rate v (S2)
#  t0 = 0.38,   # Spread for log(t0)
#  Z = 0.35     # Spread for probit(Z)
#)



2.3 Creating the GNG prior distributions
With the means and standard deviations coded for, we can now use the prior() function to generate our priors. Additionally, we also specify that this is for a non-hierarchical model.

# Creating the prior distribution for each GNG WDM parameter
priorWDMGNG <- prior(designWDMGNG,
                     pmean=pmean, 
                     psd=psd,
                     type="single") # Non-hierarchical

class(priorWDMGNG)

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 1)
text:
1. Simulating 2C and GNG data
The following section is inspired by the work of Ratcliff et al. (2018). Essentially, we are going to replicate their work by simulating two choice data (2C), turning it into Go/No-Go data (GNG) by removing reaction times from a response, and then fitting a DDM to the 2C and a GNG DDM to the GNG and seeing if the parameters are similar to each other or not.
Why do this? Well since it is the exact same dataset that is just being manipulated to not have a response time, then mathematically, the DDM should be able to generate the same parameter estimates that was used to generate it.

1.1 Specifying the 2C DDM and GNG DDM
We first start by using the design() function to specify the models we want to use. For both models, we will use the Wiener diffusion model (WDM), so that abbreviation will be used for the models. This just means that these DDMs will not estimate between-trial variability parameters (e.g., Sv, St0, SZ).
For the GNG DDM model, there is more information that we need to specify. For starters, we need to specify the ‘DDMGNG’ model within the design() function, which expects missing reaction times as a legitimate response (or in this case lack of a response). The factors argument gives the function information about our data that does not exist yet, but that is needed to make the function work (e.g., subjects and stimulus). For the Rlevels argument, we need to specify what the two response values are, we chose “TO” and “RESP” but this is arbitrary.
It is important to note that reference level of the factors will be used as the lower boundary in this model. Therefore, it is important to have “TO” as the reference (first level) for Rlevels and also to code “ng” as the reference for S.
Next we specify what parameters we want to estimate from the GNG DDM, which is the ones we estimate from a WDM. Additionally, we now have to code for information within the functions argument. The TIMEOUT represents essentially the reaction time threshold in seconds when a non-response was given- this doesn’t really matter (I don’t think) since we are changing the reaction times to NAs anyway. Next, the Rnogo argument is where we tell the design() function what the level name for R is that represents a no-go response. Similarly, the Rgo argument is the level name for R that represents a response.

# Generating the data and model specification
designWDM <- design(model = DDM,
                    factors=list(subjects=1, S=1:2), 
                    Rlevels = 1:2,                  
                    formula = list(a ~ 1, 
                                   v ~ S, 
                                   t0 ~ 1, 
                                   Z ~ 1)) 

# Generating the model specifications for a GnG dataset
designWDMGNG <- design(model = DDMGNG,
                       factors=list(subjects=1, S=c("ng", "go")),
                       Rlevels = c("TO", "RESP"),
                       formula = list(a ~ 1,
                                       v ~ S, 
                                       t0 ~ 1,
                                       Z ~ 1),
                      functions = list(
                          TIMEOUT = function(d) rep(1.5, nrow(d)),
                          Rnogo  = function(d) factor(rep("TO",   nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP")),
                          Rgo    = function(d) factor(rep("RESP", nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP"))
                        ))



1.2 Simulating the 2C and GNG data
Important: We chose a large number of trials (n = 5000 for each S) to simulate in order to get really good parameter recovery.
Here we are using the sampled_pars() function to extract a vector with the parameter names which then we populate with the parameter values we want in their respective transformed scale. We use mapped_pars() to confirm we specified the parameter values correctly and then we simulate the data using the make_data() function.
Afterwards, we take the simulated 2C data and just change it to resemble a GNG dataset. Keep in mind, there are GNG data simulating specific functions but we are not showing them in this document. They are, however, available in Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 2).

# Choose parameters for simulation, first getting a vector with the right name
parsWDM <- sampled_pars(designWDM)

# Then choosing some values. Note that we include transforms here to illustrate
# the scale on which sampling occurs
parsWDM[] <- c(log(1), -.75, 3.4, log(.3), qnorm(.5))

# Confirm our parameters were specified correctly
mapped_pars(designWDM, parsWDM)

  S     v a sv  t0 st0 s   Z SZ   z sz
1 1 -0.75 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0
2 2  2.65 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0

# Simulate the two-choide data
dat <- make_data(parameters = parsWDM, 
                 design = designWDM,
                 n_trials = 5000) # Per stimulus

Important: We must make sure that the GNG dataset has only factors and not character variables, or else fitting the DDM GNG will cause problems.

# Convert the two-choice data into GnG data
gng <- dat %>%
  mutate(S = ifelse(S == "1", "ng", "go"),
         R = ifelse(R == "1", "TO", "RESP"),
         rt = ifelse(R == "TO", NA, rt))

# Convert variables to factors (MUST DO THIS OR fit() will FAIL)
gng <- gng %>%
  mutate(
    S = factor(S, levels = c("ng", "go")),
    R = factor(R, levels = c("TO", "RESP"))
  )



1.3 Visualizing both datasets
We can use my custom functions to create a data_design object so that we can then use the functions get_descriptives() and the plotting functions plot_defectiveDensity() and plot_defectiveDensityGNG() on our datasets.
Since they are essentially the same data, we see that the accuracy and reaction times between the two are identical. Important to note, the function of the plot_defectiveDensity() function is to produce defective density plots for each stimuli in the dataset. This plot, however, makes no sense for the GNG, since within a stimulus, there is only one response with a reaction time! Thus, it is more informative to instead compare the RT distributions between stimuli, which is what the plot_defectiveDensityGNG() function does.

# Create the data_design for the two choice data
dat_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == 1 & R == 1) | (S == 2 & R == 2),
  id = subjects
)

# Create the data_design for the gng data
gng_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == "go" & R == "RESP") | (S == "ng" & R == "TO"),
  id = subjects
)

# Get the descriptives from the datasets
get_descriptives(dat, dat_design)

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 1)
section: 2. Fitting a 2C DDM and GNG DDM to the data
text:
2. Fitting a 2C DDM and GNG DDM to the data

2.1 Generating prior distributions
A deeper review for prior distributions in terms of means and standard deviations is available in the introduction to DDM guide. Note that for our purposes, we are using the same prior distribution for the 2C and GNG data. However, in practice we would expect these distributions to be different, since the GNG task itself generally results in different parameter values compared to the 2C (e.g., higher drift rate for go trials while weaker drift rate for no-go trials).
Additionally, we do need to construct two ‘emc.prior’ objects using the prior() function since they require a model design object. In other words, failing to do this will cause errors during the fitting process, even though the prior distributions between them are identical.

# Specify the prior means in the transformed scale
pmean <- c(
  a = log(1.25), 
  v = -2.2, 
  v_S2 = 2.2,  
  t0 = log(.4),
  Z = qnorm(.5) 
)

# Standard deviations
psd <- c(
  a = 0.5,     # Spread for log(a)
  v = 2.5,     # Spread for drift rate v (S1)
  v_S2 = 2.5,  # Spread for drift rate v (S2)
  t0 = 0.38,   # Spread for log(t0)
  Z = 0.35     # Spread for probit(Z)
)

# Generating the prior distributions for the two-choice data
priorWDM <- prior(design=designWDM,
                  pmean=pmean, 
                  psd=psd,
                  type="single") # Non-hierarchical

# Generating the prior distributions for the gng data
priorWDMGNG <- prior(design=designWDMGNG,
                     pmean=pmean, 
                     psd=psd,
                     type="single") # Non-hierarchical

# plotting on the natural scale
plot(priorWDM, designWDM, layout=c(2,4))










2.2 Fitting the two models
To fit the models, we first need to create ‘emc’ objects using the make_emc() function. The input for this function is the data, the model design, the priors, and whether the model is hierarchical or not. Notice the names from these different inputs have to be compatible with each other, this is why for the GNG, we needed to have its own model design and its own specific prior distribution.
After that we use the fit() function to run the Bayesian model, which can take a while so it is recommended to save the output once the model is done and then load it back into R.
Here we are naming the models as sWDM, to remind us they are Wiener’s DDM and we separate them by the task (2 choice = 2C; Go/No-Go = GNG). The s in the name just means samples.

# Create an emc object for the two-choice data
sWDM_2C <-  make_emc(data = dat, 
                     design = designWDM, 
                     type="single",
                     prior=priorWDM)

Processing data set 1


Likelihood speedup factor: 43.9 (228 unique trials)

# Create an emc object for the gng data
sWDM_GNG <-  make_emc(data = gng, 
                      design = designWDMGNG, 
                      type= "single",
                      prior=priorWDMGNG)

Processing data set 1


Likelihood speedup factor: 83.3 (120 unique trials)

# Fitting the models
# sWDM_2C <- fit(sWDM_2C)
# sWDM_GNG <- fit(sWDM_GNG)
 
# Saving the model objects
# save(sWDM_2C, file = here("ddm", "models", "sWDM_2C.Rdata"))
# save(sWDM_GNG, file = here("ddm", "models", "sWDM_GNG.Rdata"))

# Loading the model objects
load(here("ddm", "models", "sWDM_2C.Rdata"))
load(here("ddm", "models", "sWDM_GNG.Rdata"))



2.3 Checking for model convergence
Using the check() function we can see that both models converged nicely. The Rhat values are less than 1.1, which is good! Additionally all of the ESS values are much larger than 1,000. For a review on the interpretation of these values, please visit the introduction to DDM guide.

check(sWDM_2C)

Rhat    1    1.001     1    1.002    1.001

2.4 Extracting Model Parameter Estimates
Here we use the mapped_pars() function to remind ourselves what parameter values were chose (ground truth) to simulate the data. With the credint() function, we can see that both the 2C DDM and the GNG DDM recovered essentially the same parameters!
This is what Ratcliff et al. (2018) showed in their work, that a GNG DDM can capture the same information as a regular 2C DDM, thus the interpretations between the two should be comparable.

# Print the original parameter estimates
mapped_pars(designWDM, parsWDM)

section: 3.2 Plotting the predicted datasets over our original data
text:
3.2 Plotting the predicted datasets over our original data
We can use these predicted datasets to generate defective density and cumulative defective distribution plots. However, because this is a GNG task, we will only see one distribution within each stimulus, which is either a correct go response or an incorrect ng response. Regardless by comparing the data along with the predicted datasets, overall the model looks like it is doing a good job in explaining our data!
This is largely due to just how large we decided to make our data. Again, we created a dataset with 10,000 trials- had this been smaller these plots would have looked a lot worse. This is just a proof of concept that our GNG WDM can explain our data well in the right conditions!

# plotting predicted values as a density plot
plot_density(gng, ppWDM_GNG, factors = c("S"))







# Plotting the predicted values as a cumulative defective function
plot_cdf(gng, ppWDM_GNG, factors = c("S"))









3.3 Examining accuracy capture
Below we can also just check correct go and incorrect ng responses (false alarms) for the original data and the predicted datasets- in our case both the go and ng response is within the 95% CI from the predicted datasets.

# Getting descriptives for the original data
agg1 <- aggregate(R=="RESP"~subjects*S, gng, mean)
colnames(agg1)[3] <- c("RESP")
agg2 <- aggregate(RESP~S, agg1, mean)

# Getting descriptives for the predicted datasets
agg1_pp <- aggregate(R=="RESP"~ S*subjects*postn, ppWDM_GNG, mean)
colnames(agg1_pp)[4] <- c("RESP")
agg2_pp <- aggregate(RESP~S*postn, agg1_pp, mean)
agg3_pp <- aggregate(RESP~S, agg2_pp, median)
low_pp <- aggregate(RESP~S, agg2_pp, function(x) quantile(x, 0.025))
upp_pp <- aggregate(RESP~S, agg2_pp, function(x) quantile(x, 0.975))

agg4_pp <- data.frame(
   S      = agg3_pp$S,
  "2.5%"  = low_pp$RESP,
  "50%"   = agg3_pp$RESP,
  "97.5%" = upp_pp$RESP,
  check.names = FALSE  
)

agg2; agg4_pp

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 1)
text:
4. GNG WDM parameter recovery

4.1 Simulating and fitting a GNG DDM
We now need to confirm that we can recover the parameters from the GNG WDM. This is because it is possible to generate data similar to our original data from multiple combinations of parameter estimates. Thus, if we can recover very similar parameters from simulated data using our initial model estimates, then that means we can be more confident our model is working as intended.
Anyway, here we use the make_data() function to simulate data using the GNG WDM estimated parameters, turn it into an emc object and then fit the model to it.

# Simulate data from our model parameters
sim <- make_data(parameters = sWDM_GNG,
                 design = designWDMGNG,
                 data=gng)

# Make an emc object
sim_sWDM_GNG <- make_emc(data = sim,
                         design = designWDMGNG,
                         type="single",
                         prior = priorWDMGNG)

Processing data set 1


Likelihood speedup factor: 81.3 (123 unique trials)

# Fit the model to the simulated data
# sim_sWDM_GNG <- fit(sim_sWDM_GNG)

# Saving the model object
# save(sim_sWDM_GNG, file = here("ddm", "models", "sim_sWDM_GNG.Rdata"))

# Loading the model object
load(here("ddm", "models", "sim_sWDM_GNG.Rdata"))

Here we use the recovery() function to assess how similar the parameters from the original GNG WDM and the one fit to the simulated data are to each other. It is a perfect recovery.


4.2 Comparing the simulated DDM params to ground truth

# Save the original parameters from the model (in transformed scale)
ground_truth_params <- credint(sWDM_GNG)[[1]][,"50%"]

# Compare parameters from the original to the simulated data
recovery(emc = sim_sWDM_GNG, 
         true_pars = ground_truth_params)

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 2)
text:
1. Correctly simulating GNG data
Like in the previous guides, we will only be fitting Wiener diffiusion models (WDM), which is a DDM where between-trial variability parameters (e.g., Sz, St0, SZ) are not estimated. Thus our model objects (emc objects to be specific) will have ‘WDM’ in the name.

1.1 Specifying a GNG WDM
We start by creating a model design object (‘emc.design’) using the design() function where we specify that we will be fitting a ‘DDMGNG’, what the factors of our dataset will be (e.g., esubjects, S), what the responses will be (“TO” is the reference so it will map to the lower boundary), our WDM specifications within formula, and additional information about what values within R correspond to a go vs a no-go response.

# Generating the model specifications for a GnG dataset
designWDMGNG <- design(model = DDMGNG,
                       factors=list(subjects=1, S=c("ng", "go")),
                       Rlevels = c("TO", "RESP"),
                       formula = list(a ~ 1,
                                      v ~ S, 
                                      t0 ~ 1,
                                      Z ~ 1),
                       functions = list(
                         TIMEOUT = function(d) rep(1.5, nrow(d)),
                         Rnogo  = function(d) factor(rep("TO",   nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP")),
                         Rgo    = function(d) factor(rep("RESP", nrow(d)), levels = c("TO", "RESP"))
                        ))



1.2 Choosing the GNG WDM parameter values
Here we use the sampled_pars() function to extract an empty vector of parameter names that will be estimated. We then choose what these values will be and confirm that we did this correctly with the mapped_pars() function.

# Choose parameters for simulation, first getting a vector with the right name
parsWDMGNG <- sampled_pars(designWDMGNG)

# Then choosing some values. Note that we include transforms here to illustrate
# the scale on which sampling occurs
parsWDMGNG[] <- c(log(1), -1, 4.2, log(.3), qnorm(.5))

# Confirm our parameters were specified correctly
mapped_pars(designWDMGNG, parsWDMGNG)

   S TIMEOUT Rnogo  Rgo    v a sv  t0 st0 s   Z SZ   z sz TIMEOUT.1 Rnogo.1
1 ng     1.5    TO RESP -1.0 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0       1.5       1
2 go     1.5    TO RESP  3.2 1  0 0.3   0 1 0.5  0 0.5  0       1.5       1




1.3 Simulating Racliff et al. (2018) GNG data
We are using Ratcliff et al. (2018) same data structure from their study to generate our GnG data. Their GNG task had 960 trials for each subject, where 720 trials were ‘go’ trials (75%) and 240 trials (25%) were ‘no-go’ trials. Thus we will do the same but just for one subject, as we will not be fitting hierarchical models in this document.
When simulating the data, we must make sure that all of our non-numeric variables are factors and not characters, and we must make the reference level consistent with the emc model object, such that “ng” and “TO” are the reference levels.

# Specify task structure
n_trials <- 960
prop_nogo <- 0.25

# Calculate number of Go and No-Go trials
n_nogo <- round(n_trials * prop_nogo)
n_go   <- n_trials - n_nogo

# Create simulation framework
GNG_framework <- data.frame(
  trials = seq_len(n_trials),
  subjects = factor(1),
  S = factor(
    sample(c(rep("go", n_go), rep("ng", n_nogo))),
    levels = c("ng", "go")
  ),
  R = factor(
    rep(NA_character_, n_trials),
    levels = c("TO", "RESP")
  )
)

# Simulate the gng data
gng <- make_data(data = GNG_framework,
                 parameters = parsWDMGNG, 
                 design = designWDMGNG) 



1.4 Getting descriptives from the GNG data
We can use the data_design() custom function to be able to use the get_descriptives() function to get some nice descriptives of our GNG data. We can see the number of trials, the proportion of which are correct within stimulus type (‘ng’, ‘go’) and information on reaction times.

# Create the data_design for the gng data
gng_design <- data_design(
  stimulus = S,
  response = R,
  rt = rt,
  correct = (S == "go" & R == "RESP") | (S == "ng" & R == "TO"),
  id = subjects
)

# Get the descriptives from the datasets
get_descriptives(gng, gng_design)

Here we can use the plot_defectiveDensityGNG() function to compare the reaction time distribution between ‘go’ (correct) and ‘ng’ (incorrect) trials.

# Plot the defective density info
plot_defectiveDensityGNG(gng, gng_design)

3. Fitting a GNG WDM Model

3.1 Making an emc object and fitting the GNG WDM
Before we can fit the model, we need to create an emc object using the make_emc() function. For this, we input the data, the model design, the prior distribution and mention that we are fitting a non-hierarchical model. Afterwards, we can use the fit() function to run the model.

# Create an emc object for the gng data
sWDM_GNG2 <-  make_emc(data = gng, 
                       design = designWDMGNG, 
                       type= "single",
                       prior=priorWDMGNG)

title: Introduction to Go/No-Go Drift Diffusion Models (Part 2)
section: 4. Does the GnG WDM capture the data well?
text:
4. Does the GnG WDM capture the data well?

4.1 Producing the predicted values
To assess whether our model can explain our data well, we can use the predict() function to produce 50 predicted datasets. Each one is the same dimension as our original GNG dataset and contains the same number of trials for each stimuli. Essentially. we can use these datasets to generate an ‘average’ predicted dataset, made up by values in the 50th percentile and also create a 95% credible interval using values at the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles.

# Use the predict function to obtain the fitted values

3. Fitting the GNG WDM

3.1 GnG data preparations
Before we can fit the GNG DDM to the datasets, we need to do some data cleaning to prevent errors down the line. First, we need to make sure that the non-numeric variables within the datasets are factors- this is a must. Moreoever, we should code “ng” and “TO” to function as the reference level, since that is what the model will map the lower boundary to. Lastly, reaction time must be in seconds, not milliseconds!

# Rename the rt to show it is in milliseconds
gng_speed_renamed <- rename(gng_speed, rt_ms = rt)
gng_accuracy_renamed <- rename(gng_accuracy, rt_ms = rt)

# preparing the gng data for model fitting
gng_speed2 <- gng_speed_renamed %>%
  mutate(subjects = factor(1),
         S = factor(S, levels = c("ng", "go")), # have 'ng' as reference (lower boundary)
         R = factor(R, levels = c("TO", "RESP")), # have 'TO' as reference (lower boundary)
         rt = rt_ms/1000) %>% # must be in seconds
  select(trial_num, subjects, S, R, rt) # drop rt_ms

gng_accuracy2 <- gng_accuracy_renamed %>%
  mutate(subjects = factor(1),
         S = factor(S, levels = c("ng", "go")),
         R = factor(R, levels = c("TO", "RESP")),
         rt = rt_ms/1000) %>%
  select(trial_num, subjects, S, R, rt)



3.2 Fitting the GNG WDM
Here we fit the models to the data. Just like in previous examples, we need to create emc objects which we can do using the make_emc() functions and then run the model using the fit() function. We are using the same priors and model design that we created in the previous section.

# Create an emc object for the two-choice data
sWDM_GNG_spd <-  make_emc(data = gng_speed2, 
                          design = designWDMGNG, 
                          type="single",
                          prior=priorWDMGNG)
